The Problem

Northern Health is running a housing company inside a health authority. And it's costing more every year.

Five compounding problems — each one adding layers of management, cost, and liability that don't belong in a health system.

What happens as Northern Health adds units and locations?
01
108 Beds. 18 Hospitals. No Shared Infrastructure.
Each bed is a separate landlord, a separate agreement, a separate problem. What works in Prince George doesn't apply in Fort St. John. The portfolio has grown — but the system underneath it hasn't.

●●●●●●●Fort St. John

●●●●Dawson Creek
●●●Prince Rupert
●●●●●●●●●●●●●●●●●●●●●●+ 13 more sites
108 beds · 18+ landlords · 0 unified systems
02
One Unit. Ten Tasks. And They Never Stop.
Adding a single bed isn't a single decision — it's a chain. And every step requires a person, a signature, or a follow-up. Multiply that by 108 beds across 18 communities and you have a full-time operation with no dedicated operator.
Find a unit
↓
Inspect & negotiate
↓
Sign lease & onboard staff
↓
Manage maintenance & disputes
↓
Admin · renewals · turnover
↓
Repeat — every time staff change
03
One Province. Eighteen Communities. Each One a Separate Housing Market.
The geography alone makes this unmanageable without a regional operator. Vacancy rates, landlord availability, local pricing — none of it transfers between communities. Every site is effectively started from scratch.

04
One Internal Team. Responsible for All of This.
There's no operator built to deliver institutional healthcare housing at regional scale — so Northern Health absorbs every responsibility internally. Short stays, long stays, wellness, childcare, community programming — it stacks onto a team that was never resourced for it.
Short-term staff accommodation
Long-term lease management
Maintenance & unit upkeep
Childcare coordination
Community & wellness programming
Staff onboarding (housing side)
Lease renewals & turnover
Landlord disputes & compliance
05
A Paycheck Gets Them Here. Everything Else Is Why They Don't Stay.
Staff aren't choosing between salaries — they're choosing between lives. $3.8M in retention incentives addresses one factor. The communities that win the talent war are the ones offering the full picture: housing, childcare, wellness, and a reason to put down roots.

Opening — Rapport & Time-Setting

First 5 minutes. Warm, direct. Let Steve set the tone.

SAY THIS

"Hey Steve — great to catch up. Björn speaks highly of you. Really glad we could get time together."
"We've only got an hour — I want to make the highest and best use of it. Before I get into anything, I want to hear from you first: how has the new role been going? You're a few months into the portfolio now — housing, childcare, infrastructure. How's that sitting?"

THEN LISTEN

Let Steve talk. He'll surface the pain himself — admin overload, the Dawson Creek hospital question, childcare gaps, the scale of the portfolio. Don't rush past this. The more he says, the easier your job gets.

DISCOVERY QUESTIONS — USE 1 OR 2

"18 hospitals across the entire province — what does the housing admin side of that actually look like for your team day-to-day?"Opens the operational pain conversation.
"Childcare — are you hearing that from every community, or is it more concentrated in certain regions?"He'll say every community. That's your segue.
"The new Dawson Creek hospital — has housing come up in those conversations internally yet?"If not, you plant the urgency. If yes, you're already aligned.

Problem Frame — Mirror It Back

Don't present a problem they don't recognize. Reflect what Steve just told you.

THE REFRAME

"What I'm hearing — and I think it's exactly what we've seen across the province — is that Northern Health is running a property management company inside a health authority. And that's not what you signed up for."
"Every unit you add creates another landlord relationship, another lease, another maintenance call, another set of keys. The system doesn't get more efficient as you grow — it gets heavier. And the people who feel that most aren't landlords. They're your housing coordinators, your ops team, your VP."
"And then on top of that: childcare. Every community, every posting. Same answer. Same gap."

NUMBERS TO DROP — NATURALLY

$39.2M deficit. $3.8M in retention incentives — 477 staff at $8K each — and the vacancy numbers are still going up. GoHealth nursing hours doubled in 12 months. Up to 60% rural vacancy in some regions.
"The incentives patch one variable. The people who stay long-term — and who bring others — need the whole picture. Housing. Childcare. Community. A reason to actually put down roots."Pause here. Let it land before you move to solution.

CHECK-IN

"Does that resonate with what you're seeing?"Simple. Gets a nod. Locks alignment before you pivot.

The ERS Story — What We've Built

Five years in. Real assets, real team, real track record.

WHO WE ARE

"We've been doing this for five years. What it looks like in practice is asset management, strategic real estate investment, and a strong operational team — single-family units, multifamily assets, and now we're developing purpose-built facilities specifically designed for healthcare housing at scale."
"34 units under management. 6 hospitals served. $105 a night — roughly 40% below what health authorities typically spend on hotel blocks. 24/7 support, single invoice."

THE SHIFT

"But what we're building toward is bigger than that. The scale opportunity isn't unit-by-unit. It's infrastructure — hospital-adjacent hubs that combine housing, childcare, community, and wellness in one facility. The kind of place where staff don't just have a bed. They have a life."
"And here's what's different about the ERS model: as we grow, costs go down. Services go up. Your admin load goes to zero. That's the inverse of what happens when a health authority manages this internally."

CHECK-IN

"Is that a model Northern Health has seen anyone attempt at this scale in BC?"Answer is no. That's the point.

The Reveal — Dawson Creek Is Already Happening

This isn't a concept. Show him the project is real and moving.

LAY IT OUT

"In Dawson Creek, we have our first healthcare housing hub currently at 60% schematic design — ready to be financed. Tom Kenny, BOS Architecture. DMSA signed. On Hospital Road, walking distance to the new DCDH."
"Lakeview Credit Union is at the table — bridge financing, construction mortgage, takeout. The McKenzie Trust has a $250K grant submitted. Mayor, seven councillors, the MP, the MLA, the Chamber — all engaged and on record in support."
"YMCA BC is the childcare delivery partner. University of Waterloo PhD research team on health and wellness programming."

THE TURN

"What we're proposing to Northern Health is actually that you're the health authority anchor for this project. The lenders are at the table. The community is behind it. What the project needs — and what the lenders need to see — is Northern Health signalling intent."This is the pivot from presentation to ask. Say it clearly and then stop talking.

IF STEVE ASKS ABOUT THE BOARD

"Housing and childcare was elevated to a board strategic priority last October — that didn't happen by accident. The appetite is there. What moves a board is a credible partner with a real plan — not another presentation about what might be possible."

The Ask — Simple, Specific, Low-Commitment

Make it easy to say yes. No lawyers. No board process. Just direction.

ASK ONE

"What we're asking for isn't handing over the portfolio. It's Dawson Creek, one year, one master lease — a 12-month pilot to prove the model works. Low commitment. High signal."
"An MOU to signal intent — that's an executive sign-off, not a board approval. Lawyers aren't needed on day one. We can have a draft to you by end of this week. Lenders need something in 30 days."

ASK TWO — THE CFO HOMEWORK

"I want to ask one thing of your CFO and finance team: put together the true all-in cost of housing in the Dawson Creek region right now — the housing cost, the admin cost, the management overhead, the turnover cost. What is the status quo actually costing per year? When we see that number together, the MOU becomes a very easy conversation internally."This is the smartest ask in the meeting. It makes NH build the business case for you. Deliver it clearly.

TIMELINE

"Our timeline: MOU in 30 days for the lenders. From there we work toward a start date for the lease, and we align the project business plan directly to the hospital's staffing needs. We know DCDH is over 100 beds — we want to make sure what we're building is sized right for what they'll need at opening and at full capacity."

Objections & Close

Anticipate the slow-downs. Have the answers ready.

IF STEVE SAYS: "This will take time to move through governance"

"A 30-day window with a real reason behind it — lenders, construction mortgage, project momentum — that's exactly what moves committees. Vague timelines die in committees. A real deadline doesn't."

IF STEVE ASKS: "What is Northern Health's operational liability in the pilot?"

"Northern Health occupies. ERS operates. The keys hand off on day one. You get one invoice, one point of contact, and zero landlord calls. That's the model."

IF STEVE ASKS: "What if it doesn't work out?"

"It's a 12-month lease. One region. The downside is we learn something together. The upside is you move an entire region of housing off your operations plate and prove a model that scales across every NH community."

THE CLOSE

"Steve — I think we're aligned here. The project has everything it needs except one thing: Northern Health at the table. An MOU gets us there. We'll have a draft to you by end of the week."
"What do you need to see from us to feel confident taking this to your team?"Final open question. Listen. Then stop talking.
